explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The verse says, “The idols of Egypt will tremble before Him…” Think about that for a second. Gods people bowed to, and they're the ones shaking. The LORD shows up on a swift cloud and the idols can't even stand still.

explanations.answer: They will be carried off to Babylon
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this message mentions Babylon, friend. The verse says the idols of Egypt will tremble before Him, and that's where it stops. No moving trucks, no road trip. The trembling is the whole picture here.

explanations.answer: They will be hidden in the temples
explanations.explanation: Hiding is a good guess, and I know a little something about hiding. But the verse never says the idols go anywhere. It says they will tremble before Him. They're standing right there, shaking in plain sight.

Melt is the word, baker. The verse says the hearts of the Egyptians will melt within them. I know melting. I've seen what happens when the oven door stays open. This is a heart going soft from the inside.

Rejoice is a happy word, friend, and this verse is not a happy moment. The LORD is coming to Egypt, and the text says the hearts of the Egyptians will melt within them. That's fear, not a party. Save the rejoicing for later in this passage.

Rest sounds nice, doesn't it? But the verse doesn't hand anybody a pillow. It says the hearts of the Egyptians will melt within them. Nobody is relaxing when the LORD comes riding in on a swift cloud.

explanations.answer: Idols and spirits of the dead
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The LORD says they will “resort to idols and spirits of the dead, to mediums and spiritists.” (Isaiah 19:3) Their plans are frustrated, so they go knocking on the same doors again. I think that's like redialing a number that already didn't answer. They just keep dialing.

The verse never mentions Cush, friend. It says they will resort to idols and spirits of the dead, to mediums and spiritists. Once their plans fall apart, they turn inward to those things. No foreign kings get a phone call here.

Good thinking, but nobody from Jerusalem is on the guest list here. The text says they will resort to idols and spirits of the dead, to mediums and spiritists. That's who they run to when their plans fall apart. No priests, no help from Jerusalem.

Harsh is right, baker. The Lord GOD of Hosts says He will deliver the Egyptians into the hands of a harsh master, and a fierce king will rule over them. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the passage. It's plain words about a hard time coming.

Gentle would be a lovely master, friend. It's just not the one in this verse. The text says a harsh master, and then adds a fierce king who will rule over them. The picture here is hard, so let's not soften it.

Patient masters are the kind everybody hopes for, baker. This verse says the opposite. The Egyptians are delivered into the hands of a harsh master. And the next line adds a fierce king, so patient is nowhere in sight.

You got it, baker. The verse says, “The waters of the Nile will dry up, and the riverbed will be parched and empty.” For Egypt, the Nile is the big river everything runs along. When it's empty, everybody feels it. That's why the rest of this message keeps going back to the riverbed.

Good memory, friend. The Nile did turn to blood back in Moses' day. Moses was Israel's leader (Exodus 7:20). But this message says something different: the waters of the Nile will dry up, and the riverbed will be parched and empty.
A flood is the opposite problem, baker. This verse says the waters of the Nile will dry up. The riverbed ends up parched and empty. There's no water going anywhere, let alone over the land.

Nobody's throwing a party on the riverbank, friend. The text says the fishermen will mourn, and all who cast a hook into the Nile will lament. Those who spread nets on the waters will pine away. It's the reverse of celebrating.

That's right, it's false. Verse 8 says the fishermen will mourn, all who cast a hook into the Nile will lament, and those who spread nets on the waters will pine away. When the river dries up, the people who work it feel it first. Sad folks, not party folks.

explanations.answer: Reveal what the LORD has planned
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The message says, “Let them tell you and reveal what the LORD of Hosts has planned against Egypt.” So the counselors claim wisdom, and the message asks them to show it. It's like a baker who says they know the recipe, so I say: bake the thing. The question stays hanging in the air.

explanations.answer: Bring the Nile back to life
explanations.explanation: That would be a big job, friend. But the message asks something else. It asks the wise men to tell and reveal what the LORD of Hosts has planned against Egypt. Fixing the river isn't the dare in this verse.

explanations.answer: Make peace with the land of Judah
explanations.explanation: Judah comes up later in this passage, baker, but not here. Here the message asks where the wise men are now. Then it dares them to tell and reveal what the LORD of Hosts has planned against Egypt. That's the whole challenge.

explanations.answer: The LORD poured it into her
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says, baker. “The LORD has poured into her a spirit of confusion.” It's a heavy line, so I'll just say it plainly. The confusion in Egypt's leaders doesn't come from anywhere else in this verse.

explanations.answer: Her idols poured it into her
explanations.explanation: The idols are in this message, friend, but not as the ones doing the pouring. Verse 1 has them trembling before Him. Verse 14 says, “The LORD has poured into her a spirit of confusion.” So the text names the LORD.

Assyria is a mighty empire, and it shows up near the end of this passage. Here it isn't the one pouring, baker. The verse says, “The LORD has poured into her a spirit of confusion.” The text names the LORD as the one who poured it.

True, baker. The verse says, “There is nothing Egypt can do—head or tail, palm or reed.” Head or tail, palm or reed covers everybody, from the top to the bottom. It's a closed door on every side. I think that's a heavy thing to hear, so let's let it sit a moment.

Nope, this one's true, friend. The verse says, “There is nothing Egypt can do—head or tail, palm or reed.” Head or tail, palm or reed means everybody, top to bottom. No one gets an exception in this verse.

Judah it is, baker. The verse says the land of Judah will bring terror to Egypt. Whenever Judah is mentioned, Egypt will tremble over what the LORD of Hosts has planned against it. Imagine hearing one name and your knees start knocking.

Moab is a fair guess, friend, but it's not in this verse. The text says the land of Judah will bring terror to Egypt. Egypt trembles whenever Judah is mentioned. Every time that name comes up, they feel what the LORD of Hosts has planned.

Edom doesn't show up in this verse, baker. The land that brings terror to Egypt is Judah. Whenever Judah is mentioned, Egypt will tremble over what the LORD of Hosts has planned against it. So the name to remember is Judah.

That's the one, baker. Verse 18 says five cities in Egypt will “swear allegiance to the LORD of Hosts.” Remember the idols that were trembling in verse 1. Now whole cities are pledging themselves to Him. What a turn.
You'd expect that, friend, since Pharaoh is Egypt's king. But the verse says those five cities will swear allegiance to the LORD of Hosts. They aren't pledging to a throne. They're pledging to Him.

Assyria comes up later in the passage, baker, but not here. The verse says five cities in Egypt will swear allegiance to the LORD of Hosts. They're speaking the language of Canaan while they do it. No Assyrian king gets that pledge.

True, baker. Verse 20 says, “When they cry out to the LORD because of their oppressors, He will send them a savior and defender to rescue them.” Egyptians cry out, and the LORD sends a rescuer. That's the whole exchange, right there in the text.

Actually, this one is true, friend. The verse says, “When they cry out to the LORD because of their oppressors, He will send them a savior and defender to rescue them.” They call out, and He sends help. The text doesn't leave them crying alone.

It's the other way around, baker. Verse 21 says, “The LORD will make Himself known to Egypt, and on that day Egypt will acknowledge the LORD.” So Egypt doesn't refuse Him. The text says they acknowledge Him.

That's right, it's false. The verse says the LORD will make Himself known to Egypt, and on that day Egypt will acknowledge the LORD. They worship with sacrifices and offerings. After all that trembling, this is quite a change.

That's right, baker. The verse says, “He will strike them but heal them.” Then it adds that they will turn to the LORD, and He will hear their prayers and heal them. The strike isn't the last word in this verse. The healing is.

Leaving is a natural guess, friend, but the text goes another way. It says, “He will strike them but heal them.” And then, “They will turn to the LORD, and He will hear their prayers and heal them.” He doesn't walk off. He hears them.

Scattering isn't in this verse, baker. It says the LORD will strike Egypt with a plague, and then He will heal them. They turn to the LORD, and He hears their prayers. The verse ends with healing, not scattering.

Worship is right, baker. The verse says, “The Egyptians and Assyrians will worship together.” Remember, Assyria is a mighty empire, and a highway runs between the two lands. Two groups walking that highway to worship side by side. That's a picture worth looking at twice.

Fighting sounds like the usual story, friend. But verse 23 says the Egyptians and Assyrians will worship together. The highway between them is for going back and forth. No fighting here, just worship.

Trade is a clever guess with a highway in the picture, baker. But the verse says what they do together, and it's worship. “The Egyptians and Assyrians will worship together.” The highway leads somewhere better than a market.

That's the heart of it, baker. The LORD says, “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance.” Egypt is called His people, and Assyria is called His handiwork. That's a whole lot of belonging in one sentence.

Enemies would've been a safe guess earlier in this passage, friend. But the last verse changes the sound completely. The LORD of Hosts blesses them, saying, “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance.” Those are words for His own.

Israel is in the blessing, baker, but it isn't sitting above anybody. The LORD says, “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance.” Egypt and Assyria are called His. Nobody is named a servant of somebody else.
